ethiopia.summary: Amnesty International has called for an investigation into artillery strikes by Ethiopia's military and its allied Tigray Peace Forces (TPF) on civilian neighborhoods in Alamata, Tigray, from September 26 to 28, which resulted in numerous civilian casualties. The organization reported that at least 14 civilians were killed, with many more injured, as the Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF) and TPF shelled the city, disregarding the safety of its 80,000 residents. Amnesty's findings indicate that the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) also endangered civilians by establishing military bases in populated areas, including schools. Despite the TPLF's denial of wrongdoing, Amnesty emphasized that such actions do not excuse the ENDF's indiscriminate use of artillery in civilian areas, which violates international humanitarian law. Eyewitness accounts and investigations revealed that many attacks targeted residential homes and public spaces, leading to significant civilian suffering and loss of life.

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Needs Political Reconciliation, Not Another Military Victory - Ethiopia Insight
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Needs Political Reconciliation, Not Another Military Victory - Ethiopia Insight About Alerts Contact Donate Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Telegram Ethiopia Insight • Independent • Informed • Incisive • Home News Analysis ARIF In-depth Viewpoint Insights Videos Viewpoint Ethiopia Needs Political Reconciliation, Not Another Military Victory 24 November, 2026 Ermias Amare SUPPORT ETHIOPIA INSIGHT What Tibor Nagy’s insights reveal about Ethiopia’s political choices. Ambassador Tibor Nagy and I go back more than two decades. Our paths crossed long before today’s political debates, through development work, education, and a shared attachment to Ethiopia. Following the Ethio-Eritrean war, I designed the USAID-funded Doha Resettlement Project. I still remember visiting it with Ambassador Nagy to observe its progress. Those were different days, but they marked the beginning of a relationship and conversations about Ethiopia that have continued for more than twenty years. Nagy’s contribution to Ethiopia extended beyond conventional diplomacy. During his tenure as U.S. ambassador, he helped strengthen relationships between American and Ethiopian universities. Those partnerships opened doors for young Ethiopian academics, including some of us teaching at Ethiopian universities, to pursue graduate studies in the United States. I was one of those fortunate beneficiaries. So was Getachew Reda. Our paths eventually diverged. Getachew returned home and remained deeply involved in his country’s affairs. I chose the relative comfort and opportunities of building my life and career in the United States. But physically leaving Ethiopia and emotionally leaving Ethiopia are two different things. Not a day has gone by without my thinking about my motherland. I have continued to follow its triumphs and tragedies, argue about its politics, and write about a country I still deeply care about. Perhaps that is why Nagy and I have continued talking about Ethiopia all these years. I have shared a Texas steak with him in Lubbock and had countless conversations about Ethiopia, Africa, Washington, and the complicated politics of the Horn. We agree on much and disagree on important matters. But I have never questioned his affection for Ethiopia. Nagy served as U.S. ambassador to Ethiopia from 1999 to 2002 and later as assistant secretary of state for African affairs. Having previously served at the U.S. Embassy in Addis Ababa, he has maintained a close interest in the country long after leaving government. His experience also gave him an interesting perspective on something many Ethiopians misunderstand: Washington. In a recent interview , he joked about the tendency of Ethiopians to imagine that the president of the United States wakes up thinking about Ethiopia and goes to bed thinking about Ethiopia. Sometimes, he said, he simply laughs at that perception. The point is not that Ethiopia is unimportant. With its enormous population, history, and geopolitical influence, it is a major country in the Horn of Africa. But Washington has interests across the world. Ethiopia is one important file among many. Ethiopians sometimes interpret every statement from Washington as evidence of a grand strategy designed specifically for or against their country. International politics is usually less romantic than that. Perhaps that is one reason I continue to listen when Nagy speaks, even when I disagree with him. A Needless War Many of Nagy’s views resonate deeply with me. When war broke out in northern Ethiopia in November 2020, we were both saddened. Nagy would later describe the conflict as “one of the most needless wars in history.” I couldn’t agree more. Whatever political calculations existed at the time, the human cost eventually dwarfed whatever objectives the protagonists believed they could achieve. For years, I kept asking myself: what exactly was the objective? What political goal could justify the lives lost, displacement, destruction of infrastructure, and bitterness among people who ultimately still have to live next to one another? Even at the beginning of the war, Nagy questioned the TPLF leadership’s objectives. His assessment was that the conflict was not about Tigray’s secession but rather about removing Abiy Ahmed and restoring the TPLF’s former prominence in Ethiopian politics. With hindsight, even many who once sympathized with the TPLF have reassessed those decisions. History will continue debating who did what, when, and why. The dead, however, have no such luxury. Nagy and I also find common ground on the Nile. His argument to Egypt is straightforward: this is 2026, not the nineteenth or twentieth century. The political and economic realities of the Nile Basin have changed. Ethiopia can no longer be expected to accept historical arrangements indefinitely while being denied the ability to develop water resources originating within its territory. Nagy believes recognizing this reality could produce a win-win agreement between Ethiopia and Egypt. That is precisely the approach the region needs. Egypt’s legitimate concerns about water security deserve respect, as does Ethiopia’s right to development. The Nile should not be treated as a zero-sum contest in which Ethiopia’s development automatically becomes Egypt’s loss. There is enough history between these two ancient civilizations. What they need now is a future. The same realism should apply to Ethiopia’s search for reliable and diversified access to the sea. Nagy argues that dependence on a single primary maritime corridor creates genuine economic and strategic vulnerabilities and that Ethiopia has every right to pursue mutually beneficial agreements with neighboring coastal states. But economic necessity does not confer sovereignty over another country’s coastline. A population of 120 million, or 150 million someday, does not automatically create a legal right to somebody else’s territory. Ethiopia’s solution must come through diplomacy: negotiated port access, commercial agreements, leases, infrastructure integration, and regional economic cooperation. The objective should not be taking somebody else’s sea, but making geography work for everybody. Alliances and Interests Nagy is skeptical of the alliances emerging around Ethiopia. His analysis raises an important question: what holds an alliance together once its common enemy disappears? That question is particularly relevant to the recently announced Alliance for Survival, which brought together the TPLF, a Fano faction, the Oromo Liberation Army, and other groups opposed to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government. In his interview with Meaza Mohammed of Roha TV, Nagy described it essentially as an “ alliance on paper .” Its members may share one immediate objective: opposing Abiy. But a common enemy is not the same as a common vision for Ethiopia. The contradictions are considerable. The TPLF and Fano were fighting each other only a few years ago, and serious territorial disputes remain unresolved. Their constituencies also hold sharply different views of Ethiopia’s constitutional order. The TPLF has historically defended the multinational federal arrangement it helped establish, while important strands of Amhara political thought have challenged aspects of that system. The OLA brings another political history and set of demands. Suppose the alliance succeeds in removing Abiy. Then what? How would its members resolve territorial disputes, approach ethnic federalism, settle the constitutional question, and distribute political power? A common enemy can bring yesterday’s adversaries into the same room. It cannot manufacture a common political philosophy. That is the deeper meaning behind Nagy’s description of an “alliance on paper.” Today’s common enemy does not necessarily create tomorrow’s common vision. Another Nagy observation that resonates with me is his skepticism toward the phrase “the international community.” We often speak of the international community as though it were a single government applying one coherent moral standard to the world. No such government exists. Washington, Beijing, Moscow, Brussels, Cairo, Ankara, Abu Dhabi, and Riyadh all have interests. Sometimes they converge; often they collide. International institutions such as the United Nations, World Bank, and IMF exert considerable diplomatic and economic influence, but they operate within a system in which powerful states retain disproportionate influence. For Ethiopia, the lesson is straightforward: foreign policy must be built on interests and relationships, not romantic assumptions about permanent friends or enemies. Federal Questions Nagy also challenges political assumptions that have hardened into conventional wisdom. One concerns ethnic federalism. Some Ethiopian intellectuals speak as though Ethiopia invented the concept of organizing federal units around linguistic or ethnic communities. It did not. Nagy has pointed to Switzerland, not because the two countries are identical, but because other federal systems have accommodated linguistic and cultural identities. The crucial difference lies in the institutions surrounding them. As he has essentially argued, Switzerland learned to distribute prosperity, while Ethiopia’s federal system has too often operated amid poverty and intense competition. The comparison has limits. Ethiopia is not Switzerland. But federalism itself may not be the disease; the institutions surrounding it may be the problem. I would add an important qualification. Ethnic federalism without genuine democracy can become ethnic competition institutionalized by the state. When citizens believe access to resources, employment, security, and political power depends primarily on which ethnic group controls government, federalism can magnify differences rather than manage them. Switzerland learned how to share prosperity. Ethiopia too often ended up organizing competition over poverty. Federalism requires more than drawing boundaries. It requires functioning democratic institutions, economic opportunity, minority protections, and a willingness to lose political power without fearing for one’s existence. The TPLF’s Future For all the areas where Nagy and I agree, there is one fundamental issue on which our assessments diverge: the present power and future of the TPLF. Nagy appears to believe the organization remains sufficiently intact to continue as a major political force and that some form of coexistence with the Prosperity Party remains possible. I see something fundamentally different. The TPLF’s greatest loss, in my view, is not military hardware, government offices, or even formal political authority. It is psychological. For decades, the organization fused three separate ideas into one political identity: the TPLF, Tigray, and the people of Tigray. Criticizing one was often interpreted as criticizing all three. That monopoly has been broken, and no political force has done more to dismantle it than the people of Tigray themselves. A population that endured war, displacement, hunger, and enormous loss has every right to question everyone, including the organization that governed Tigray in its name. The TPLF may retain experienced cadres, networks, loyal supporters, and political influence. But organizational survival is not the same as retaining ownership of a people’s political identity. That era, in my view, is ending. This is where I believe Ambassador Nagy may eventually revise his assessment. The Tigray he once knew politically has changed profoundly. Perhaps one day we will have another Texas steak in Lubbock and revisit this conversation. Maybe then I’ll remind him that I told him so. But rejecting the TPLF’s political monopoly does not mean endorsing the Prosperity Party. Ethiopians deserve more than a choice between old authoritarianism and new authoritarianism. They deserve peace, constitutional government, accountable institutions, freedom of expression, and a political system in which losing an election does not mean losing one’s security, livelihood, or place in the country. The federal government bears primary responsibility for protecting Ethiopia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and maintaining lawful public order. But state authority alone does not confer political legitimacy. Legitimacy must be earned. With economic hardship, armed conflicts, and deep political mistrust across several regions, Ethiopia cannot indefinitely govern its contradictions through force. It needs a credible national dialogue, not a ceremonial conference with predetermined conclusions. It needs reconciliation, accountability, and a political settlement broad enough to allow Ethiopians with fundamentally different views to live under the same constitutional roof. Other post-conflict societies offer lessons worth studying, but Ethiopia must develop a reconciliation model suited to its own history. Tigray’s Transition The political transformation underway in Tigray should not be mistaken for a finished project. The dismantling of the TPLF’s old monopoly has created an opening, but an opening is not yet democracy. The caretaker administration has an opportunity to demonstrate that political change means more than replacing one group of appointed officials with another. For decades, power in Tigray was concentrated within the ruling structure. Local leaders could be appointed, reshuffled, or sidelined from above, while political survival often depended on loyalty to the organization. Allowing communities to choose their woreda, kebele, and other local leaders would therefore represent something many have not genuinely experienced for decades: the ability to choose those who govern them. But the federal government must resist the temptation to replace one political monopoly with another. The Prosperity Party has every right to compete for Tigrayans’ support, but no entitlement to their votes. Political parties and movements across Tigray need space to organize, campaign, and present competing visions. Otherwise, control of the institutions of the state—the proverbial bank and tank—could reproduce the old problem under a different political logo. The caretaker administration should remain exactly what its name implies: a caretaker, not the architect of Tigray’s permanent political future. The question is whether Tigrayans are finally free to decide who represents them. If they choose PP, that choice should be respected. If they choose another organization, that choice must be equally respected. Democracy begins when those who control the state accept that they may not control the outcome. Recent outreach by federal officials is encouraging. Field Marshal Birhanu Jula’s visit to Mekelle and his emphasis on Tigray’s place within Ethiopia are part of a conversation that needs to continue. Tigray is not a peripheral footnote in Ethiopia’s history. Aksum, Adwa, Gundet, and Dogali are not merely Tigrayan memories; they are woven into the historical consciousness of Ethiopia itself. Separating Tigray’s history from Ethiopia’s would require tearing pages out of the same book. But historical recognition alone cannot produce reconciliation. It must be accompanied by political inclusion. The federal government must engage Tigray’s diverse political actors, including those with whom it profoundly disagrees, provided they pursue their objectives peacefully. Political integration cannot mean political assimilation. Nor should reconciliation require Tigrayans to adopt the federal government’s interpretation of recent history. Their grievances, fears, and political disagreements will not disappear simply because the balance of military power has changed. Those disagreements need somewhere peaceful to go. From Arms to Politics The remaining TPLF-aligned armed forces must also confront a changed political reality. For decades, the TPLF’s power rested on more than its military strength. It commanded an institutional architecture encompassing government, security, local administration, economic networks, and an organizational structure reaching from the highest levels down to local communities. Much of that architecture has now been dismantled. Yet some within the remaining armed movement appear to believe that retreating to rural areas or mountains and continuing an insurgency could recreate an earlier generation’s political comeback. Today’s Ethiopia is not the Ethiopia of the 1970s, 1980s, or 1991. Its political environment, technology, military capabilities, and regional circumstances have changed. History does not repeat itself simply because an organization remembers how it once succeeded. The path toward disarmament, demobilization, and civilian reintegration should remain open. Those willing to put down their weapons should not automatically be treated as permanent enemies. Subject to accountability for serious crimes and appropriate security safeguards, Ethiopia should pursue credible reintegration mechanisms allowing former combatants to return to civilian life. Where legally and politically appropriate, negotiated amnesty or other transitional arrangements could form part of a broader settlement. Reconciliation, however, must not mean impunity for grave abuses, whoever committed them. Abandoning armed struggle should not require abandoning political conviction. If the TPLF, or whatever organizations emerge from its remnants, believes it retains a constituency, there is one legitimate way to demonstrate it: go to the people. Organize peacefully, present a program, build coalitions, debate opponents, and ask Tigrayans for their votes. If they choose you, govern. If they reject you, accept their verdict. That is the transition Ethiopia needs: from the politics of the gun to the politics of persuasion. The federal government has an equally important responsibility. It cannot chase former combatants into the mountains while closing peaceful political space in the cities. A successful transition requires movement from both sides: armed groups must abandon violence, and the state must embrace genuine political inclusion. The door out of the mountains must lead somewhere: to civilian life, political dialogue, reconciliation, and ultimately the ballot box. That would not erase the past, but it might prevent another generation from having to repeat it. A Shared Principle Perhaps this is where Nagy and I ultimately come together. Political organizations come and go. Ethiopia remains. Those who imagine Ethiopia can simply be Balkanized underestimate the historical, economic, cultural, and human ties binding its peoples together. But those who believe unity can be preserved indefinitely through coercion make an equally dangerous mistake. A country is strongest when its people choose to remain together, not when they are forced to. Ethiopia’s future cannot belong exclusively to PP, TPLF, Fano, OLA, or any other political organization. Nor can it belong to one individual. It has to belong to Ethiopians. After more than twenty years of conversations with Ambassador Nagy, from development projects and university exchanges to Washington politics and Texas steaks in Lubbock, perhaps this is the principle on which we agree most: Ethiopia’s problems are ultimately political, and their lasting solutions must also be political. Dialogue, compromise, democracy, and reconciliation may lack the excitement of battlefield victories or revolutionary slogans. But after everything Ethiopians have endured, perhaps peaceful political compromise is exactly the revolution the country needs. Query or correction? ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia is at a critical juncture where political reconciliation is essential, rather than pursuing further military victories, as emphasized by Ambassador Tibor Nagy. The ongoing conflict, particularly in Tigray, has resulted in immense human suffering and loss, raising questions about the objectives behind such wars. Nagy argues that the focus should shift from military solutions to diplomatic negotiations, especially regarding Ethiopia's access to the Nile and maritime routes. He highlights the need for a realistic approach to alliances, noting that shared opposition does not equate to a unified vision for the future. Furthermore, he critiques the concept of ethnic federalism in Ethiopia, suggesting that the surrounding institutions, rather than the federal structure itself, may be the root of the problem. Ultimately, both Nagy and the author advocate for a political landscape that prioritizes democracy, accountability, and genuine reconciliation over authoritarianism, allowing Ethiopians to build a more prosperous future.

ethiopia.title: IGAD Chief Hails Ethiopia's Indispensable Role in Advancing Horn of Africa Peace, Unity
ethiopia.content: East Africa: IGAD Chief Hails Ethiopia's Indispensable Role in Advancing Horn of Africa Peace, Unity - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français East Africa: IGAD Chief Hails Ethiopia's Indispensable Role in Advancing Horn of Africa Peace, Unity 22 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) Executive Secretary Dr. Workneh Gebeyehu has hailed Ethiopia as an indispensable regional anchor. Speaking to ENA, Dr. Workneh emphasized the East African nation's strategic leadership in advancing peace, diplomacy, unity and collective action across the Greater Horn of Africa. The Executive Secretary underscored Ethiopia's longstanding commitment to regional integration and cooperation, highlighting its founding role in IGAD and its leadership in steering the regional bloc for more than eight years. He also noted that he is the second Ethiopian to serve as IGAD Executive Secretary, reflecting the country's longstanding contribution to the organization's leadership and regional affairs. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines "Ethiopia's role is indispensable. It can lead in peace, diplomacy, and bringing all member states together. We appreciate Ethiopia's role, not only in the region but also across the continent," he said. The IGAD chief stressed that Ethiopia's diplomatic influence and strategic position make it a key partner in strengthening regional solidarity, promoting dialogue and mobilizing coordinated responses to shared challenges. He also called for stronger cooperation between Ethiopia and other IGAD member states. In that regard, Workneh noted that collective commitment and joint action are essential to addressing the region's persistent challenges, particularly drought, food insecurity, peace and security threats. "If Ethiopia and the other member states come together, we can truly win the battle against drought, food insecurity, peace and security challenges, and other issues confronting our region," he said. As the region faces interconnected political, economic and climate challenges, Workneh underscored that strengthened cooperation among IGAD member states remains critical to unlocking its collective potential and building a more stable and prosperous future. ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Advances Global Peacekeeping Ambitions, Climate Diplomacy and Strategic Red Sea Aspirations
ethiopia.content: East Africa: Ethiopia Advances Global Peacekeeping Ambitions, Climate Diplomacy and Strategic Red Sea Aspirations - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français East Africa: Ethiopia Advances Global Peacekeeping Ambitions, Climate Diplomacy and Strategic Red Sea Aspirations 22 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) By Staff Writer From strengthening its legacy in international peacekeeping and preparing to host COP32 to expanding diplomatic partnerships and renewing the debate over Red Sea access, Ethiopia's engagements throughout the week highlighted its ambition to shape regional stability and play a more influential role in global affairs. Ethiopia has intensified its diplomatic, security and development engagements, projecting an increasingly multifaceted vision of its role in Africa and the wider international community. Developments throughout the week reflected the country's efforts to consolidate its longstanding contribution to international peacekeeping, strengthen its climate leadership ahead of hosting COP32 in 2027, deepen regional cooperation and advance discussions surrounding its strategic maritime interests. Together, these developments underscore Ethiopia's ambition to translate its historical diplomatic standing, growing national capabilities and development achievements into greater regional and international influence. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Seven Decades of Peacekeeping: Ethiopia Seeks to Strengthen Its Global Role Ethiopia's longstanding contribution to international peacekeeping remains a defining pillar of its foreign policy and international engagement, with the country now seeking to adapt its capabilities to an increasingly complex global security environment. Speaking at a consultative forum jointly organized by the Ethiopian National Defense Force's International Peace Support Training Institute (IPSTI) and the Ethiopian National Defense College, IPSTI Commandant Brigadier General Gezahegn Fekadu underscored Ethiopia's nearly seven-decade legacy of contributing to international peace and security. From its participation in the Korean War to subsequent peace support missions in Sudan, South Sudan and Somalia, Ethiopia has maintained a sustained presence in international and regional efforts to promote stability. However, the changing global security landscape, declining funding for peace operations and political disagreements within multilateral institutions are creating new challenges for troop-contributing countries. Gezahegn stressed that Ethiopia must strengthen its operational readiness, modernize its capabilities and establish sustainable partnerships to maintain its position as a major contributor to international peacekeeping. He also highlighted the significant progress made by the Ethiopian National Defense Force through organizational reforms, improved weaponry, advanced training and broader capacity-building initiatives. These developments, he noted, have strengthened the country's defense readiness while enhancing its ability to safeguard national interests and contribute to regional security. The strategic discussion was further reinforced by FDRE Navy Commandant Vice Admiral Kindu Gezu, who emphasized that Ethiopia's future peacekeeping engagements must balance national security priorities, international responsibilities and its enduring commitment to stability in the Horn of Africa. He described the country's peacekeeping legacy as more than an international obligation, characterizing it as a national asset and strategic legacy that should inform future engagements. The message emerging from the forum was clear: Ethiopia cannot rely solely on its historical achievements. It must continuously adapt its military capabilities, operational strategies and international partnerships to remain relevant in a rapidly changing global security environment. Securing Sovereign Red Sea Access and Its Regional Implications Alongside its peacekeeping ambitions, Ethiopia's strategic interest in the Red Sea continued to feature prominently in discussions about its long-term economic and geopolitical future. Political scientist Bizuneh Yimenu, a lecturer in Comparative Politics at Queen's University Belfast, argued that Ethiopia's maritime future should ultimately be based on sovereign ownership of a Red Sea port rather than continued dependence on access arrangements with neighboring countries. He described Eritrea's independence in 1993 and the subsequent loss of Ethiopia's coastline as a major geopolitical transformation whose implications continue to shape the country's strategic calculations. According to Bizuneh, the political process surrounding Eritrea's independence should have included separate negotiations over Ethiopia's maritime position and unresolved border questions. He maintained that the legitimacy of Eritrea's self-determination and Ethiopia's responsibility to safeguard its strategic interests were distinct matters that should have been addressed independently. The scholar emphasized that the issue should now be pursued through political dialogue, diplomacy, regional integration and negotiations rather than rigid legal or constitutional arguments. His assessment highlights the wider geopolitical and economic significance of Ethiopia's maritime aspirations, particularly for a country whose population, economic ambitions and regional responsibilities continue to expand. COP32: Ethiopia Positions Climate Leadership at the Center of Its Global Engagement On the climate diplomacy front, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed reaffirmed the government's commitment to ensuring successful preparations for COP32, which Ethiopia is scheduled to host in 2027. The Prime Minister said he convened the COP32 National Steering Committee to review progress, assess preparations and provide strategic direction for the country's hosting of the global climate summit. He called for a coordinated, whole-of-government approach, emphasizing that all task forces must work in alignment to ensure effective preparations and successful delivery of the conference. Beyond hosting a major international gathering, Abiy described COP32 as a strategic opportunity for Ethiopia to advance its environmental priorities, strengthen international partnerships, attract investment and translate ongoing national initiatives into lasting development outcomes. The summit is expected to provide Ethiopia with an important international platform to showcase its climate initiatives, development priorities and commitment to sustainable growth. For Ethiopia, COP32 represents more than a diplomatic hosting responsibility. It offers an opportunity to connect its domestic development agenda with global climate action, particularly around climate finance, green investment, renewable energy and sustainable development. GERD: A Landmark for Ethiopia's Energy Future and Regional Cooperation Ethiopia's development ambitions also received international recognition during a visit by a delegation from the United States Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) to the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD). Led by CFR President Michael Froman, the delegation described the mega-hydropower project as a remarkable engineering achievement and an important milestone for Ethiopia's economic growth, industrial development and regional energy cooperation. The visiting delegation, including Mahesh K. Kotecha, Kevin Kinsella and Michelle Gavin, expressed admiration for the project's scale, efficiency and significance. Froman acknowledged the enormous investment of time, financial resources and human effort behind the construction of the dam, describing its completion as a major accomplishment for Ethiopia and the wider region. He also highlighted its potential to generate electricity for Ethiopia and neighboring countries, contributing to broader economic development and regional energy cooperation. The visit placed the GERD in the wider context of Africa's energy transformation, demonstrating the importance of large-scale infrastructure in supporting industrialization, expanding electricity access and strengthening economic connectivity. IGAD Chief Reaffirms Ethiopia's Indispensable Regional Leadership Ethiopia's regional diplomatic significance was further underscored by Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) Executive Secretary Dr. Workneh Gebeyehu, who described the country as an indispensable anchor for peace, diplomacy and cooperation across the Greater Horn of Africa. Speaking to ENA, Workneh highlighted Ethiopia's founding role in IGAD and its longstanding contribution to regional integration and collective action. He also noted that Ethiopia has played a significant role in the leadership of the regional organization, including his own tenure as Executive Secretary for more than eight years. "Ethiopia's role is indispensable. It can lead in peace, diplomacy, and bringing all member states together. We appreciate Ethiopia's role, not only in the region but also across the continent," he said. His remarks reinforced Ethiopia's strategic importance in advancing regional solidarity, promoting dialogue and mobilizing collective responses to shared challenges. At a time when the Horn of Africa faces complex political, security and economic dynamics, Ethiopia's diplomatic influence and geographical position make its engagement central to efforts aimed at building a more integrated and stable region. New Ambassadors Signal Stronger Partnerships with Ethiopia Ethiopia's diplomatic engagement also gained momentum as President Taye Atske Selassie received the credentials of 16 newly appointed ambassadors, marking another opportunity to strengthen bilateral and multilateral relations. The newly accredited diplomats expressed their commitment to expanding cooperation with Ethiopia across trade, investment, peace and security, agriculture, digitalization, healthcare and cultural exchange. Norwegian Ambassador Yngvild Berggrav described Ethiopia as a strategic country and pledged to build on existing areas of cooperation. Finnish Ambassador Erik Lundberg and Maltese Ambassador Bernard Hamilton also expressed their commitment to further strengthening relations with Ethiopia. Meanwhile, Republic of Korea Ambassador Koo Hong-seok highlighted opportunities to attract additional South Korean investment, particularly in agriculture, digitalization and healthcare. He also paid tribute to Ethiopia's historic contribution to the Korean War, recalling the sacrifices made by Ethiopian soldiers in defending South Korea's freedom and independence. The ambassador affirmed that his country would continue supporting Ethiopian veterans and their families, while working to deepen bilateral relations. The diplomatic commitments reflect Ethiopia's continuing importance as a partner for countries seeking expanded engagement in the Horn of Africa and across the African continent. A Broader Strategic Vision In nutshell, the week's developments reveal a country seeking to strengthen its influence through multiple interconnected fronts. Its peacekeeping legacy provides a foundation for greater international security engagement, while military modernization is intended to sustain its capacity to respond to emerging threats. Its preparations for COP32 offer an opportunity to elevate its climate diplomacy and attract international investment. The GERD, meanwhile, demonstrates the country's determination to expand energy production and contribute to regional economic transformation. At the same time, Ethiopia's diplomatic partnerships and renewed maritime debate reflect its broader ambition to secure strategic interests, deepen regional integration and expand its international standing. The challenge ahead will be to translate these ambitions into sustainable outcomes through diplomacy, institutional capacity, economic cooperation and constructive regional engagement. Eventually, Ethiopia's engagements throughout the week point to a broader national aspiration: to move beyond its historical role as a major African diplomatic and security actor and strengthen its position as an influential force in shaping Africa's peace, prosperity, climate future and strategic direction. The country has a long-standing commitment to international peacekeeping, with nearly seven decades of contributions, and is adapting to a changing global security landscape by modernizing its military capabilities. Ethiopia is also preparing to host COP32 in 2027, positioning itself as a leader in climate action and sustainable development. ethiopia.title: The El Alamein–Aswan Axis and the Strategic Containment of Ethiopia - horn review
ethiopia.content: The El Alamein–Aswan Axis and the Strategic Containment of Ethiopia – HORN REVIEW Home Research and Analysis Ethiopia and the World Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Publications Horn Review Journal Articles Policy Briefs The Greater Horn: Monthly Strategic Brief Horn Review Magazine Weekly Geopolitical Report Research Paper Commentary Event Flagship Events Conferences Brainstorming Sessions Team About Us Contact Us Search Home Research and Analysis Ethiopia and the World Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Publications Horn Review Journal Articles Policy Briefs The Greater Horn: Monthly Strategic Brief Horn Review Magazine Weekly Geopolitical Report Research Paper Commentary Event Flagship Events Conferences Brainstorming Sessions Team About Us Contact Us 2026-11-23 The El Alamein–Aswan Axis and the Strategic Containment of Ethiopia 0 Comments The November 21 meeting in Aswan between the foreign ministers of Egypt, Sudan, and Eritrea consolidates a regional alignment whose political foundations were laid in El Alamein the previous month. Meeting on the sidelines of the sixth Aswan Forum for Sustainable Peace and Development, Badr Abdelatty, Mohieddin Salem and Osman Saleh reaffirmed that responsibility for Red Sea governance rests with its coastal states, expressed support for Sudan’s sovereignty and national institutions, rejected foreign-backed armed militias and renewed their backing for Somalia’s territorial integrity. Cairo’s intention to brief Mogadishu on the discussions connected the trilateral consultation to the four-state process established in October and indicated that the participating governments intended to sustain coordination beyond individual summits. Their convergence brings the Red Sea, the Nile, Sudan’s war and Somalia’s territorial dispute into a common diplomatic framework. For Ethiopia, the significance lies in the cumulative pressure this coordination can exert across several areas of its national security and foreign policy. The political framework was established on October 4, when Abdel Fattah el-Sisi hosted Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, Isaias Afwerki and Hassan Sheikh Mohamud in El Alamein. Their joint declaration addressed Sudan’s national institutions and territorial integrity, rejected parallel authorities and support for mercenaries, reaffirmed Somalia’s sovereignty and opposed recognition of or support for Somaliland. It also asserted exclusive littoral responsibility for Red Sea governance and called for prior notification, consultation and consensus over transboundary water issues, with particular reference to the existing uses of the downstream Nile states. These positions brought several distinct political disputes under a single set of principles. The declaration’s importance therefore extends beyond the individual issues it addressed. It provided the governments with common language through which to present their respective security and foreign-policy objectives as parts of a shared regional position. The establishment of a periodic follow-up mechanism gave that coordination an institutional channel, which the November meetings subsequently carried forward. The timing of the summit was particularly consequential for Ethiopia. On October 1, 2026 , Addis Ababa announced the closure of its embassy in Asmara and declared ten Eritrean diplomats persona non grata , accusing Eritrea of direct and indirect acts of hostility and the diplomats of activities threatening Ethiopian national security. The diplomatic rupture occurred amid renewed fighting in Tigray, escalating accusations of Eritrean involvement in Ethiopia’s internal conflict, and reports of Eritrean military incursions across the border into Tigray. Three days later, Eritrea joined Egypt and Sudan in a quadrilateral consultation whose agenda addressed several questions directly connected to Ethiopia’s strategic interests. The summit did not identify Ethiopia by name, but its positions on the Nile and the Red Sea were advanced in a regional setting in which Ethiopia’s disagreements with the participating governments were already intensifying. Eritrea’s participation also gave its confrontation with Addis Ababa a wider diplomatic context, linking the bilateral security dispute to Egypt’s longstanding anxiety over the Nile and the regional debate over maritime access. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s parliamentary address on October 5 brought the maritime question into this increasingly coordinated diplomatic environment. Following his reappointment, Abiy reiterated that Ethiopia would pursue reliable access to the sea through dialogue, mutual benefit and what he described as the principle of give and take. The significance of this formulation lies in its emphasis on negotiated arrangements with neighboring states. It expressed Ethiopia’s long-term strategic and economic interest in maritime access while recognizing that practical arrangements require the participation of states through whose territory access would be secured. This distinction matters because Cairo has increasingly framed Ethiopia’s maritime aspirations through the question of military access and the militarization of the Red Sea. The resulting disagreement concerns both the terms of Ethiopia’s access and the wider political authority claimed by coastal states to determine which countries may participate in maritime arrangements. Egypt’s position gives neighboring governments a common basis for opposing certain forms of Ethiopian engagement, while Ethiopia’s position rests on its right to pursue negotiated access under international law. The November 2 Egypt–Sudan 2+2 consultation in Cairo translated this broader political alignment into more specific bilateral positions. Bringing together the two countries’ foreign and irrigation ministers, the third round of the mechanism addressed the Nile, Red Sea security and Sudan’s war in a single engagement. The joint statement reaffirmed Egypt and Sudan’s coordination over their downstream water interests, described the GERD as a unilateral action contrary to international law, and called for prior notification, consultation and consensus. It also invoked the 1959 Nile Waters Agreement and reaffirmed the Permanent Joint Technical Commission as the instrument through which the two governments coordinate their positions. On the Red Sea, the statement asserted exclusive responsibility for coastal states and rejected maritime access for non-littoral countries where it would compromise coastal sovereignty, territorial integrity or port security. The convergence of these issues is important. The bilateral mechanism gives Cairo and Khartoum an organized platform for coordinating their positions on matters that also feature in the wider El Alamein and Aswan consultations. It allows Egypt to advance its Nile and maritime priorities alongside Sudan’s security concerns, while giving Khartoum diplomatic support in its relations with Ethiopia. The legal difficulty with the November 2 statement begins with its invocation of the 1959 Nile Waters Agreement as the basis for protecting the two governments’ existing water uses. Concluded between Egypt and Sudan, the agreement established a bilateral allocation framework that assigned 55.5 billion cubic meters annually to Egypt and 18.5 billion cubic meters to Sudan under the arrangements negotiated by the two parties. Ethiopia did not participate in those negotiations and did not consent to the agreement. Under the principle reflected in Article 34 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties , a treaty creates neither obligations nor rights for a third state without its consent. The 1959 agreement therefore remains relevant to the bilateral relationship between Egypt and Sudan, but its allocations cannot be imposed on Ethiopia or treated as a basin-wide settlement governing the rights of all riparian states. Cairo and Khartoum may coordinate their claims under that agreement, but the agreement itself cannot determine Ethiopia’s entitlement to equitable and reasonable use of the Nile. The wider body of international water law provides a different basis for organizing relations among the riparian states. The 1997 UN Convention on the Law of the Non-Navigational Uses of International Watercourses articulates the principles of equitable and reasonable utilization, cooperation and the obligation to take appropriate measures to prevent significant harm. It also provides for the exchange of information, notification of planned measures and consultations aimed at reaching an equitable resolution where states raise concerns. These principles require Ethiopia to take downstream interests seriously through transparent data exchange, technical coordination, dam safety measures, and impact-management arrangements, commitments Ethiopia is already fulfilling. They also require Egypt and Sudan to recognize Ethiopia’s right to develop and utilize the waters of a shared international river. The principle of no significant harm is a due-diligence obligation that operates alongside equitable and reasonable utilization. It does not establish a guarantee of zero impact or confer a permanent veto on downstream states over upstream development. Prior notification and consultation are important legal procedures, while consensus remains a political objective for cooperation rather than a universal condition granting every downstream government control over the development choices of another riparian state. The same legal limitation applies to Egypt and Sudan’s attempt to confine the GERD question to the three Eastern Nile states. Ethiopia, Sudan and Egypt have direct interests in the dam’s construction, filling and operation, and their participation in negotiations over its management is both necessary and consistent with the principles of cooperation under international water law. Their geographical designation as the three Eastern Nile states, however, does not establish an exclusive legal authority over the wider basin or give them the competence to determine the rights and interests of other riparian countries. International watercourse law, particularly the principles of equitable and reasonable utilization, sovereign equality and cooperation, recognizes the rights and corresponding responsibilities of all riparian states in the use, development and protection of shared water resources. Articles 5 and 8 of the 1997 UN Convention on the Law of the Non-Navigational Uses of International Watercourses articulate these principles, while Article 7 establishes the obligation to take appropriate measures to prevent significant harm. These obligations require states to consider one another’s interests, exchange relevant information and pursue consultations where planned measures may produce significant adverse transboundary effects. They do not confer on a group of downstream states general authority to determine the development rights of upstream countries or make their consent an unconditional prerequisite for the latter’s utilisation of shared waters. The three Eastern Nile countries can therefore establish arrangements for the management of the GERD through direct negotiations, but those arrangements cannot constitute the exclusive legal framework governing the interests of the wider Nile Basin. The same legal limitation applies to the position advanced by Egypt and Sudan that the GERD question should be confined to the three Eastern Nile states. Ethiopia, Sudan and Egypt have direct interests in the dam’s construction, filling and operation, making trilateral negotiations over its management both necessary and consistent with the principles of cooperation under international water law. Such negotiations, however, must be distinguished from an assertion that the three countries possess exclusive authority over the wider Nile Basin. Their geographical designation as the Eastern Nile states does not confer the competence to determine the rights and interests of other riparian countries or to establish an exclusive framework for basin governance. International watercourse law, particularly the principles of equitable and reasonable utilization, sovereign equality and cooperation, recognizes the rights and corresponding responsibilities of all riparian states in the use, development and protection of shared water resources. Articles 5 and 8 of the 1997 UN Convention on the Law of the Non-Navigational Uses of International Watercourses articulate these principles, while Article 7 establishes the obligation to take appropriate measures to prevent significant harm. These principles require states to consider one another’s interests, exchange relevant information and pursue consultations where planned measures may produce significant adverse transboundary effects. They do not confer on Egypt and Sudan, or on the three Eastern Nile states collectively, a general authority to determine the development rights of other riparian countries or make their consent an unconditional prerequisite for the latter’s utilization of shared waters. Trilateral arrangements for the management of the GERD are therefore legitimate and necessary, but they cannot be treated as the exclusive legal or institutional framework governing the interests of the wider Nile Basin. The Cooperative Framework Agreement (CFA) , which entered into force on October 13, 2024, provides an institutional expression of this broader approach to basin governance. Following ratification by Burundi, Ethiopia, Rwanda, Tanzania and Uganda, and accession by South Sudan, the agreement established a legal framework for cooperation among its participating riparian states. Ethiopia’s signature and ratification of the CFA reflect its commitment to developing common basin-wide arrangements based on equitable and reasonable utilization, sustainable development and cooperative management. This commitment has also been reflected in Ethiopia’s efforts to engage other Nile Basin countries in the GERD process, including its invitation to riparian states to attend the dam’s inauguration. Such engagement acknowledged that the interests surrounding the dam extend beyond the three countries directly involved in its construction and operation and that its development should be considered within the wider context of basin cooperation. Sudan’s political and military situation provides another important dimension of the alignment. In the November 2 statement, Egypt reaffirmed its support for Sudan’s national institutions and invoked the bilateral Joint Defense Agreement as a basis for taking measures permitted under international law to protect Sudan’s territorial integrity. The statement specifically identified the Sudanese Armed Forces as central to the country’s national security, including its water security. This position reflects Cairo’s longstanding preference for maintaining a strong relationship with the Sudanese military leadership, whose authority is central to Egypt’s security calculations along the Nile and its southern border. The SAF is Sudan’s regular national army, and Egypt’s support for it cannot be equated automatically with backing a militia. Yet the war has placed the army within a wider struggle over political authority and the future structure of the Sudanese state. Material and diplomatic support for its leadership therefore has consequences for the balance of power in the conflict and for the prospects of a civilian-led settlement. Egypt’s commitment to Sudanese national institutions is consequently inseparable from the political and military position of the leadership currently exercising state power. The security implications extend beyond the diplomatic support expressed in joint statements. Reuters reported in February 2026 that Egyptian officials had acknowledged providing logistical and technical assistance to the SAF, while satellite imagery showed Turkish-made Bayraktar Akinci combat drones at the East Oweinat airfield inside Egyptian territory near the Sudanese border. Egyptian officials told Reuters that military equipment had been supplied to southern airports for border security and to support possible military action in defense of national security. Cairo denied accusations of direct involvement in airstrikes against RSF forces, The evidence nevertheless shows that Egypt’s relationship with the SAF has acquired a significant operational and material dimension. This raises questions about the relationship between Cairo’s declared opposition to foreign interference in Sudan and its own growing involvement in the military environment surrounding the conflict. Egypt’s support may be presented as assistance to the recognized national army, but it also strengthens one side in a war whose political resolution requires an inclusive Sudanese process. The question of foreign support for armed actors also tests the principles advanced at El Alamein and reaffirmed in Aswan. The October declaration rejected interference in internal affairs, support for mercenaries and the establishment of parallel authorities, while the November trilateral meeting rejected the foreign arming of militias. Yet the regional security environment described by independent conflict monitors points to relationships between governments and armed opposition networks that complicate these commitments. In its June 2026 assessment of the Tigray conflict, ACLED reported indications of Eritrean support for the TPLF and other insurgent groups, including the Amhara Fano National Movement, through the Tsimdo initiative. It also reported that a conference held in Port Sudan in May brought together actors linked to the Eritrean government, the SAF leadership, dissident factions of the Ogaden National Liberation Front, prominent Amhara nationalists and other armed opposition groups. The wider pattern is a proxy engagement, in which governments invoke sovereignty to condemn external involvement in their own security affairs while maintaining relationships with actors who challenge the authority of neighboring governments. The principle of non-interference can retain credibility only when applied consistently by all states. Egypt’s record in Libya further illustrates the relationship between sovereignty principles and shifting strategic interests. Cairo has been one of the most prominent external backers of Khalifa Haftar’s eastern-based military forces, which have competed with the western-based authorities in Tripoli for control of the Libyan state. Its engagement with Haftar was shaped by border security and the balance of power in Libya, but it also involved support for a military center of power operating against the authorities in the west. Egypt’s reopening of its embassy in Tripoli in November 2026, after a twelve-year closure, marked a rapprochement with the western-based administration. The shift demonstrates Cairo’s capacity to recalibrate its relationships as political and security circumstances change. That flexibility is understandable as an instrument of foreign policy, but it also means that the principles of non-interference and support for national institutions advanced at El Alamein should be assessed against Egypt’s own history of involvement in the Libyan conflict. The sovereignty of states cannot be treated as an absolute principle when it constrains Ethiopia and a flexible consideration when Egypt’s own regional interests are at stake. Eritrea’s earlier engagement with Somaliland presents a more specific example of the distinction between diplomatic principle and political practice. In March 2019, Foreign Minister Osman Saleh and presidential adviser Yemane Gebreab visited Hargeisa to initiate direct engagement with Somaliland’s authorities. The visit did not amount to formal recognition, and that distinction must be maintained. It nevertheless demonstrated Asmara’s willingness to establish relations with Somaliland’s de facto administration as part of its regional diplomacy. The El Al
ethiopia.summary: The recent meeting in Aswan among the foreign ministers of Egypt, Sudan, and Eritrea marks a significant step in regional alignment aimed at containing Ethiopia's influence. This trilateral consultation, which followed a prior summit in El Alamein, emphasized the governance of the Red Sea by its coastal states and reaffirmed support for Sudan's sovereignty and Somalia's territorial integrity. The discussions reflect a coordinated diplomatic effort to address shared concerns, particularly regarding the Nile and Red Sea security, amidst rising tensions involving Ethiopia. Ethiopia's recent diplomatic rupture with Eritrea and its ongoing internal conflicts further complicate the situation. The joint statements from these meetings highlight a commitment to prior notification and consultation over transboundary water issues, particularly concerning the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD). However, the legal basis for these agreements raises questions, as Ethiopia was not part of the 1959 Nile Waters Agreement, which Egypt and Sudan reference to assert their claims. International water law principles advocate for equitable utilization and cooperation among all riparian states.

ethiopia.summary: United Bank for Africa (UBA) has decided to postpone its banking expansion plans in Ethiopia due to concerns regarding Nigeria's 10% cap on foreign investments. The bank's management indicated that the regulatory environment in Nigeria poses challenges for its international growth strategy, particularly in expanding its operations in Ethiopia. This decision reflects the broader implications of Nigeria's investment restrictions, which can hinder the ability of financial institutions to diversify and tap into emerging markets. UBA's focus on maintaining compliance with local regulations has led to a reevaluation of its expansion timeline. The bank's leadership remains committed to exploring opportunities in Ethiopia but must navigate the complexities of investment policies in Nigeria before proceeding. This situation highlights the impact of national regulations on the strategic decisions of banks operating in multiple countries.

ethiopia.title: Health Financing Top of Agenda As African Leaders Meet in Addis
ethiopia.content: Africa: Health Financing Top of Agenda As African Leaders Meet in Addis - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Africa: Health Financing Top of Agenda As African Leaders Meet in Addis 23 November 2026 The New Times (Kigali) By Joan Mbabazi African leaders and health experts began a five-day meeting in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, on Monday, November 23, to discuss ways of reducing the continent's dependence on foreign health financing and imported medical supplies. ALSO READ: PM Nsengiyumva in Addis for Africa public health summit The fifth International Conference on Public Health in Africa (CPHIA 2026) brought together heads of state and government, health ministers, researchers, scientists and development partners. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Co-hosted by the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) and the Government of Ethiopia, the conference is held under the theme, "Africa's health security and sovereignty: Transformation from health dependency and vulnerability to ownership and resilience." Rwanda is represented by Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva, who is attending on behalf of President Paul Kagame, alongside Minister of Health Dr Sabin Nsanzimana and technical delegations. More than 30,000 participants are expected at the conference, whose programme features 189 sessions across six thematic tracks. Among the high-level participants and speakers are Africa CDC Director-General Dr Jean Kaseya, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, Ethiopian Health Minister Dr Mekdes Daba and WHO Regional Director for Africa Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi. The meeting comes as African countries face growing pressure to finance their health programmes amid declining external assistance. According to Africa CDC, external health aid to the continent was projected to decline by about 70 percent between 2021 and 2025. Public health emergencies also increased by 41 percent, from 152 in 2022 to 213 in 2024. The funding concerns have renewed calls for governments to increase domestic investment in healthcare and reduce reliance on donor-funded programmes. Participants will discuss how countries can develop long-term, nationally financed health investment plans and ensure that external support is aligned with their priorities. They will also examine ways of improving government oversight of health programmes and making funding more predictable. Health financing is important given that only three African countries, Rwanda, Botswana and Cabo Verde, have met the Abuja Declaration target of allocating at least 15 percent of their national budgets to health, according to Africa CDC. There was a problem processing your submission. Please try again later. Access to medicines, vaccines and diagnostic products is another major item on the agenda. African countries continue to rely heavily on imports, exposing their health systems to supply disruptions and limiting access to essential products. The conference will examine ways of expanding local pharmaceutical and vaccine manufacturing, improving regulatory systems and increasing investment in research and technology. Africa has set a target of producing at least 60 percent of its vaccine needs locally by 2040. Discussions will consider how countries can attract investment, build manufacturing capacity and improve regional cooperation to achieve this ambition. The continent's influence in global health decisions will also feature, with participants examining reforms to the global health architecture and how African countries can advance their priorities in international forums, including the World Health Organisation (WHO), the World Trade Organisation and the United Nations General Assembly. The programme also includes discussions on pandemic prevention and preparedness, primary healthcare, digital health, artificial intelligence and the effects of climate change on health security. Several continental health initiatives are scheduled to be launched during the conference. These include the African Union Champions' Roadmaps on Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health for 2026-2030, scheduled for Monday. On Tuesday, participants will launch the Continental Immunisation Forum and the inaugural Continental AIDS Monitoring Report. Discussions on the CPHIA Health Financing Pathway Compact are also scheduled. The meeting will conclude on Friday, with discussions on African-led research and development, global health security and the future of primary healthcare. Read the original article on New Times .
